waves.1: `connect`, `by`, `measure`, `step` with its first rule (spring) — fourteen sequences build on the kernel as it is plus these
waves.3: the remaining `step` rules (ca, verlet, boids, learn) and `field`
waves.4: synthesis — no new construction: compare the grammar, turn its parameters, rewrite it

kernel.connect: a relation between two NAMED parts of one compose — drawn as a line it is an edge, with a step rule it is a spring, with a number it is a weight. `{"op":"connect","a":"n1","b":"n2"}`. Both builders. First, because forces (7) needs it long before graph theory (21) names it
kernel.by: the parameter function f(index, t): `{"by":{"fn":"list|sine|noise|random|lerp", …}}` — on an array it is `vary` (t = 0: colour, height, rotation, phase per part); on an engine it is motion (the same function with t running). One implementation serves both
kernel.replicate: one replication operator with four presets — array (X → X X X X shifted), times, recurse (X → n transformed copies of X, bounded `depth`: the only place self-containment is allowed) and rewrite (a string rule, generations; the turtle is its interpreter)
kernel.step: the neighbourhood engine: a named rule applied per part from its neighbours and connects — spring, field, boids, ca, verlet, learn share one interface. ONE verlet in both renderers (SoftBody3D cannot squeeze; Jolt only for the rigid fall that exists), so the two sides cannot drift
kernel.field: a solid from a function of space: a scalar field over a grid → marching cubes (iso); union / subtract / intersect as min / max of distance fields (boolean) — to be checked against the boolean_surfaces halls before the CSG nodes are dropped
kernel.measure: the instrument half of the grammar (Palle, 23 Oct: "add measure as the sixth piece"): a value READ off a thing — a length, a count, an entropy, a projection, a loss — `{"op":"measure","of":{…},"what":"length|count|entropy|…"}`; RETAINED across steps as a record, a trail, a history (the sibling of `trace_data`, which carries what a visitor meant); and COMPARED with another under a stated rule (`{"op":"compare","a":…,"b":…,"rule":…}`). It is what the spine's principles mostly say — compare (104), measure (67), retain (45) of the 420 — and no construction says it. Shown as a label, a bar or a readout beside the thing it reads; both builders

connect: the two parts' right to differ — a spring pulls them alike; the difference it removes each tick is the leak
spill: the displacement a spring undid
by: everything between two parts: f is sampled at integers, the curve between them is never built
spill: the curve between the samples, as points
every other sequence the seed did not choose
replicate: the copies past the bound — MAX_DEPTH 24 in builder.gd; the Cantor set's fourth removal (EDGE_INVENTORY: deadband at 0.01 m)
spill: the transforms of the copies not built
a copy smaller than the floor — the level at which a fractal stops being a picture of itself
spill: the sub-floor copies, as points
step: what happens between two ticks — the rule refuses on its own time
every neighbour outside the radius (boids, verlet): one region, every arrival alike
spill: the neighbours a part did not see
the stiffness, speed or force past the clamp
measure: everything finer than the instrument reads — a length to the millimetre, an entropy to two decimals; the thing has more than the reading
spill: the residual, as a number the bus does not rank
what the record forgets — a trail keeps the last N, a history the last T; the earlier passage is gone from the end you are not watching
what the rule equates — two things compared as lengths lose the right to differ in everything but length
no spill — the rule is named, which is the whole lesson
field: every value under the threshold — the field exists there and no surface is drawn
the subtracted volume — a body that is never seen; boolean's remainder is the clearest leak in the kernel
spill: the subtracted volume, as points
the surface between grid cells (marching cubes interpolates, it does not know)

transformation.text: Changing position, orientation or size changes possible passage. Ask which properties survive each operation and which body the resulting space admits.

Compare body-driven openings with timed obstacles.
Name invariants precisely: translation and rotation preserve distances; uniform scale preserves angles and proportions, not lengths; non-uniform scale can change shape.
Observe the still cube before collecting it; three moving demonstrations remain. Add translation, rotation and scale, then climb to four finished pickups.
Compare translation, scaling and rotation as crossings, without the head crab. Move the far bank while the plank keeps its motion: what makes the crossing possible?
Thirteen pickups sit on seven carrier routes through x, y and z. Two exit mechanisms share a destination but permit different journeys; the turning torus anticipates rotation.
Compare a level Y bridge and upright X/Z rides, two body widths in rotated arrays, a tunnel and five carousel profiles. Which dimensions make space for this body?
Take the bottle: the room changes to four times its size in one update, then your body is relocated onto the table. Descend and compare the enlarged doorway with a fixed museum frame.
Approach turns slats and shrinks blocks; contact cuts an open-topped trench in a low lattice. Step clear to see reversible openings return; the cut remains.

Timed pushers, rotating slabs and synchronised growers change access on level ground. At the exit, two armoured door leaves combine translation, rotation and scale into a passage that opens on approach.
